summaries.example: Maya tells her brother, “I promise I will save you a seat.” Her words may make him count on her. Philosophers ask why this promise creates a special duty for Maya, why the duty is mainly owed to her brother, and what happens if keeping it becomes difficult.
summaries.summary: Promises seem simple: someone says they will do something, and other people expect them to follow through. Philosophers study why this creates a moral obligation. A promise is unusual because it is voluntary—you do not have to make one—but after making it, you may have a duty to keep it. The duty is also special: it is owed especially to the person who received the promise. Promises help people plan, trust one another, cooperate, and form agreements. Different theories explain their force in different ways. One says people have a special power to create duties by choosing. Another says promises work because communities have shared rules. A third focuses on the expectations or trust created in the other person. Other philosophers say a promise is a commitment made between people. The entry also connects promises with contracts, law, speaking, vows, and oaths.
key_ideas: People usually think promises should be kept.
Promises help people trust one another and work together.
A promise creates a special duty to the person who received it, not exactly the same duty we have toward everyone.
Philosophers disagree about what makes a promise binding: a person’s choice, shared rules, another person’s expectations, or a commitment made together.
Promises are voluntary, but once made they may limit what the promisor should choose later.
summaries.why_it_matters: Promises are part of everyday life. Friends, families, schools, businesses, and governments all depend on people being able to count on one another. Thinking about promises helps us understand trust, fairness, agreements, and why our choices can create responsibilities.

important_terms.definition: A promise is a serious statement that you will do something, or not do something, in the future.
An obligation is something a person ought to do. A promise can create an obligation for the person who makes it.
Trust means counting on someone because you believe they will act as they said they would.
A convention is a shared way of doing things that helps people understand and coordinate with one another.

questions_to_think_about: Should a promise always be kept, even when keeping it causes a serious problem?
Can you make a real promise to yourself?
Does a promise count if the other person never hears or accepts it?
Why might a community need people to keep promises?

summaries.example: Suppose Alex promises Jordan a ride home. Later, Alex receives an attractive invitation to do something else. One view says Alex has a duty because Alex voluntarily gave Jordan a special claim or authority. Another says the duty depends on the shared practice of promising. An expectation-based view emphasizes that Jordan was led to rely on the ride, while a commitment view treats the promise as an interpersonal commitment. The case also raises questions about whether the duty remains if Jordan never expected the ride or releases Alex from it.
summaries.summary: The philosophical problem of promising is not merely whether promises should usually be kept. It is how a voluntary act can generate a moral obligation, often directed toward one particular person. The main approaches differ over the source of this normative force. Normative-power theories treat promising as an ability to alter one’s normative circumstances directly. Older versions connect this power with virtue or natural law; more recent versions appeal to interests in freedom, cooperation, authority, or relationships. Conventionalist theories emphasize the social practice of promising. They may claim that the practice makes promises intelligible, supplies their rules, gives them moral force, or performs more than one of these roles. Expectation theories explain obligation through what promises do to promisees: they may provide assurance, invite reliance, or invite trust. These views face challenges involving circularity, the difference between promises and other ways of influencing people, and cases in which the promisee cannot form the relevant response. Interpersonal theories instead analyze promises as joint commitments or second-personal transactions involving authority to make claims. The entry also examines how these theories bear on contracts and law, speech-act theory, consequentialism, and unusual cases such as self-promises, vows, oaths, and promises to the dead.
key_ideas: Promises are voluntary acts that can create directed obligations: duties owed especially to particular promisees.
Normative-power theories say a promisor directly changes the moral situation through an intentional promise, often because people benefit from self-binding, cooperation, authority, or relationships.
Conventionalist theories appeal to the institution or practice of promising. Some distinguish the rules that make promises intelligible from the reasons those rules are morally binding.

Expectation theories focus on assurance, reliance, or trust. Critics ask whether expectations are sufficient, whether the account becomes circular, and how it handles promises to people unable to respond.
Interpersonal theories describe promising as a joint commitment or as a transaction grounded in second-personal authority.
Theories of promises also affect debates about speech acts, contracts, consequentialism, vows, oaths, promises to oneself, and promises to the dead.
summaries.why_it_matters: A theory of promising helps explain a basic structure of moral and social life: people can take on responsibilities through voluntary communication. Promises support planning and cooperation, but they can also conflict with later interests or consequences. The debate therefore tests broader views about rights, authority, trust, social practices, personal agency, and the relationship between morality and law.

important_terms.definition: A moral obligation is a requirement about what one ought to do. Promissory obligations are usually directed particularly toward the promisee.
A normative power is an ability to change duties, rights, or permissions through an intentional act, such as making a promise.
Conventionalism explains promises by appealing to a shared social practice or system of rules that makes promising possible or binding.
Expectation theory holds that promises generate duties through expectations, reliance, or trust created in the promisee.
Uptake is the promisee’s receiving, recognizing, accepting, expecting, relying on, or trusting the promise, depending on the theory.
A joint commitment is a commitment made by people together, rather than merely several separate personal commitments.
A second-personal obligation is a duty connected with one person’s authority to make claims or demands on another.
Rule consequentialism evaluates rules by their consequences; it can defend promise-keeping because a reliable practice may produce better overall results.

questions_to_think_about: If a promise creates no expectation or reliance, is there still an obligation to keep it?
Does the shared practice of promising explain what a promise is, why it is binding, or both?
Can a person create an obligation simply by deciding and speaking, or must another person accept the promise?
Should a theory of promises explain vows and oaths as well as ordinary promises?
How should a consequentialist handle a promise whose breach would produce better results than its fulfillment?

summaries.example: Lena promises her friend Sam that she will bring the science-project poster tomorrow. Sam plans the presentation around that promise. A theory about expectations says Lena’s duty is connected to the confidence she created in Sam. A conventionalist theory says the shared rules of promising make Lena’s statement count as a promise. A normative-power theory says Lena used her own choice to create a special duty. Another theory says Lena and Sam now share an interpersonal commitment. These explanations may agree that Lena should bring the poster, while disagreeing about why.
summaries.summary: Promises are important because they allow people to create trust, coordinate plans, and enter agreements. The central philosophical question is why making a promise can create an obligation. Promissory obligations have two unusual features. They are voluntary: people are not generally required to promise. Yet after a promise is made, the promisor may be required to keep it. They are also directed toward a particular promisee rather than owed equally to everyone. One family of theories describes promising as a normative power: by intentionally promising, a person changes the duties and claims involved. Another family is conventionalist. It explains promises through a shared practice, whose rules may make promising possible and may also help justify keeping promises. Expectation theories focus on the promisee. A promise may give assurance, encourage reliance, or invite trust, and breaking it may wrong the promisee by disappointing or betraying that response. Critics question whether expectations can explain every promise and whether an expectation-based explanation becomes circular. Interpersonal theories understand promises as joint commitments or arrangements in which people gain authority to make claims on one another. These disagreements extend to contracts, speech acts, legal rules, consequentialism, vows, oaths, and promises to oneself or to someone who cannot respond.
key_ideas: Promises are usually seen as voluntary, but they can create duties once they are made.
Promissory duties are directed: they are owed especially to the promisee, unlike some general duties such as not harming people.
Some philosophers say promising directly changes a person’s moral situation; others say its force depends on social rules, expectations, or relationships.
Expectation theories differ over whether the promisee must merely seek assurance, actually rely on the promise, or develop trust.
A major challenge is explaining promises made to people who cannot respond or form expectations, such as someone who has died.
Promises are related to contracts and law, but philosophical theories do not all explain their connection in the same way.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding promises helps us think clearly about trust and responsibility in friendships, families, schools, law, and public life. It also shows why a simple sentence can have moral significance: what matters may be the speaker’s choice, the social practice, the listener’s response, or the relationship created between them.

important_terms.definition: An obligation is a duty or requirement about what someone should do. A promissory obligation is created or connected to making a promise.
A promisee is the person to whom a promise is made. A promisor is the person who makes it.
A normative power is the ability to change what one ought to do, or what another person may claim, through a voluntary act such as promising.
A convention is a shared practice or set of rules that helps people understand actions and coordinate their behavior.
Expectation theory explains a promise’s force through the assurance, reliance, or trust it creates in the promisee.
A joint commitment is an obligation or plan that people form together, not merely separate promises made by each person alone.
An uptake condition is a requirement concerning whether the promisee notices, accepts, expects, relies on, or trusts the promise.
Consequentialism judges actions or rules by their results. A consequentialist may defend promise-keeping because reliable promises often have good effects.

questions_to_think_about: If Sam did not hear Lena’s promise, would Lena still have the same duty?
Is relying on a promise different from merely believing it?
Could a promise be valid even when the promisee cannot understand it?
Why might promise-keeping be important even when breaking a promise would bring a useful result?
Are promises to yourself genuine promises, or are they a different kind of commitment?
